articles.title: IKEA y Xbox presentan una colección de productos gaming que no parecen gaming y que querrás tener en casa
articles.text:
IKEA y Xbox han presentado en la Gamescom una colección de productos para casa inspirada en los elementos icónicos de Xbox que ofrece una vuelta de tuerca a lo que se considera un espacio gaming. Una fusión entre las filosofías de ambas compañías que trasciende el concepto que tenemos de espacio gaming para abrirlo a cualquier estancia del hogar.
XSTABY, que así se llama la colección, está compuesta por siete productos que se alejan de esa estética gaming oscura y con RGB para abrir la puerta a un diseño más amable con cualquier espacio y, sobre todo, mucho mejor integrado en cualquier hogar. A simple vista, es una fusión de elementos icónicos de Xbox con el diseño nórdico y sencillo de Ikea, en el que cada producto está tremendamente bien pensado y con una función muy definida, pero que a simple vista no parece, desde luego, un producto "gamer".
Esta colaboración nace precisamente del cambio que están experimentando los espacios de videojuegos, que cada vez más están virando hacia espacios más compartidos donde no tiene que ser todo exclusivamente gamer. Aquí es donde entra ese saber hacer de IKEA de simplificar un diseño a simple vista, pero que en realidad esconde más de lo que parece. La propuesta es, por tanto, sencilla: una colección enfocada al gaming, pero que permita adaptarse a cualquier salón o estancia de la casa cuando el gaming se termina.
IKEA XSTABY: Una colección gamer que no parece gamer
Quizás los tres ejemplos más característicos de esta colección que llevan esa idea a su máximo esplendor son el XSTABY VISSLE, un sillón gaming que se adapta a diferentes posturas, pero que a simple vista es todo lo contrario de lo que podrías imaginarte cuando escuchas la palabra sillón gamer: es sencillo, sobrio y discreto, pero esconde algunos elementos como un espacio dedicado para guardar tus mandos. O la mesa auxiliar gaming XSTABY, que a simple vista encajaría con cualquier estancia o salón, pero que en su interior esconde un sistema totalmente enfocado a servir de centro de carga para tus mandos y para organizar los cables de tu consola.
Lo mismo sucede con el que quizás sea el producto más interesante de toda la colección: su mueble de TV con ruedas YXSTABY. Permite colgar tu tele en un soporte con un diseño exquisito y poder moverla a cualquier punto de casa. El sistema está pensado, además, para esconder todos tus cables, y cuenta con una balda con rejilla trasera para colocar tu consola Xbox, y ganchos para sus mandos y auriculares. Nada queda a la vista, todo queda recogido y colocado de forma perfecta para favorecer la ventilación de la consola y ofrecer un espacio amable a la vista y alejado del desorden. Y con la posibilidad de poder cambiarla de ubicación en la estancia o llevártela a cualquier punto de casa sin necesidad de desmontar o quitar nada. Además, la TV queda a la altura perfecta para jugar y combinar con el sillón YXSTABY.
La colección incluye, además, otros accesorios más pequeños, pero igualmente bien pensados. Para los más coleccionistas, IKEA también ha presentado un expositor de mandos con un soporte que permite exponer tus mandos de Xbox en el salón de casa o en tu espacio gaming.
Y no solo para los mandos, el expositor permite quitar el soporte para el mando y usarlo para exponer tus productos favoritos. También un nuevo soporte para monitor que a su vez incluye un soporte para el mando.
Para los más fans de Xbox, quizás los productos más icónicos de esta colección son los más interesantes. Un taburete diseñado a medida y semejante a un stick de Xbox, que además está disponible en dos colores, negro y verde Xbox; una bandeja inspirada en el accesorio para el pad del mando Xbox Elite, que es bastante llamativa y está disponible, al igual que el pad, en acero inoxidable; y un cojín gaming (para usar mientras sujetas el mando de la consola en tus sesiones de juego) inspirado en X de Xbox.
YXSTABY, precio y disponibilidad
La colección de IKEA y XBOX, YXSTABY, estará disponible en las tiendas de IKEA a partir del próximo 1 de octubre de este mismo año, con los siguientes precios:
- YXSTABY Cojín gaming tipo botón direccional 14,99€
- YXSTABY Taburete palanca direccional: 39,99€
- YXSTABY Bandeja gaming de botón direccional: 14,99€
- YXSTABY Minivitrina para mandos gaming: 19,99€
- YXSTABY Sillón gaming VISSLE: 99€
- YXSTABY Soporte para monitor gaming: 29,99
- YXSTABY Mueble de TV gaming con ruedas: 99€
- XSTABY Mesa auxiliar gaming con ruedas: 129€
- YXSTABY Soporte portátil gaming con almacenaje: 24,99€

articles.title: The Download: the Kids issue arrives, and Bill Gates reveals his AI fears
articles.text:
The Download: the Kids issue arrives, and Bill Gates reveals his AI fears
Plus: Trump’s EPA aims to exempt data centers from disclosing air pollution.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Introducing: the Kids issue
If the desire to limit kids' use of technology was once a subcurrent, it has become a raging flood. Countries around the world are banning children from social media. Schools across the US are ditching iPads and Chromebooks for actual books. Kids themselves seem to be embracing this tech skepticism too: the hottest gadget for Gen Alpha is a vintage Sony Walkman.
A surprising—maybe troubling—number of people who work in big tech also keep their kids at arm’s distance from technology. They lock down their phones, if they have phones at all, and keep them off social media. Hell, even Mark Zuckerberg doesn’t publicly post his children’s faces on Facebook or Instagram.
Yet there is no hiding from technology. It permeates nearly everything, everywhere. We have to prepare our children to live in the actual world we have actually created, not the one we wish we had. How can we help kids survive and thrive in what we have wrought?
That's what the new Kids issue of MIT Technology Review is all about. With the help of the editors of Anyway, a fantastic magazine for teens and tweens, we explore how young people really feel about AI, the support networks helping kids through the polycrisis, and what happens when a child's robot best friend dies.
We also ask why kids outlearn AI, whether monitoring apps are really keeping children safe online, how schools can encourage smarter AI use, and what happens when technology begins to reshape childhood itself, courtesy of exclusive new fiction from author and AI ethicist Jenny Williams.
Together, these stories examine how childhood is changing in an age of AI—and how we can help kids navigate the world we've made. Subscribe now to read the print issue in full.
Bill Gates says we’ve passed AI’s danger thresholds. Now what?
—Mat Honan
It’s a glorious day in Kirkland, Washington, an affluent Seattle suburb on the eastern shore of Lake Washington. The temperature is in the mid-80s, the sky is incapable of being any more blue, and the view is gorgeous. And vaguely terrifying.
Because if the scene is placid, the messenger is not. Seated across from me at a conference room table, Bill Gates is rocking back and forth in his chair. And the more he has to say—about the threats of terror or economic collapse or just losing control of our AI systems—the more agitated I find myself becoming, too.
The philanthropist and former Microsoft CEO says he has been growing increasingly alarmed by the rate at which AI technology is advancing, especially since guardrails are not keeping pace.
“We’ve crossed the threshold in terms of [AI’s] bio-capabilities, cyber-capabilities, psychosocial capabilities, job-market-destruction capabilities, and even the lack of control,” he said. “I’m just stunned at the lack of concern and discussion outside of the industry.”
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Trump’s EPA aims to exempt data centers from disclosing air pollution
The EPA would also remove requirements for public input. (NYT $)
+ The move is likely intended to curb criticism and oversight. (Guardian)
+ Texas’s attorney general has joined the data-center backlash. (WP $)
+ We did the math on AI’s energy footprint. (MIT Technology Review)
2 SpaceX plans $100 billion launch site in Louisiana—its largest yet
Construction of the “Starbase, Louisiana” project is due to start next year. (BBC)
+ It would be SpaceX’s second private launch site, after the original Starbase. (NYT $)
+ The company said it will “support thousands of launches” annually. (CNBC)
+ But it’s cutting launches from Florida until Starship arrives. (Ars Technica)
3 China’s Z.AI has confirmed it’s behind the mystery AI model Ox Alpha
The model has surged to the top of online usage charts. (Bloomberg $)
+ China’s Moonshot is discussing a landmark deal with US hyperscalers. (Reuters $)
+ Here’s what’s next for Chinese open-source AI. (MIT Technology Review)
4 Meta is discussing a settlement in its landmark teen-addiction trial
The case involves 29 states seeking penalties and changes. (Reuters $)
+ A loss at trial could saddle Meta with $1.4 trillion in penalties. (Bloomberg $)
5 Huawei wants to build data centers in Egypt
The US is alarmed and is preparing a counteroffer. (Bloomberg $)
+ HP has signed a licensing deal for Huawei WiFi tech. (CNBC)
6 Trump is upping the price of Big Tech’s favorite visa
He’s implementing a fee of over $103,000 on H-1B visas. (Verge)
+ His immigration policies are hurting young researchers. (MIT Technology Review)
7 Beijing fears that AI companions are replacing human intimacy
New rules aim to limit emotional dependence on chatbots. (Guardian)
+ It’s surprisingly easy to fall for a chatbot. (MIT Technology Review)
8 Israel is running a synthetic think tank to influence AI search results
It’s using AI-generated content to shape chatbot responses. (404 Media)
9 Physicists are closing in on a way to test string theory
A proposed dark dimension could be detectable within five years. (Economist $)
10 AI music has been barred from the Australian charts, thanks to Madonna
An AI-assisted cover of “Like a Prayer” helped prompt the ban. (Reuters $)
Quote of the day
“It is such an Orwellian technology being utilized by such comic book villain forces of evil trying to do dastardly things.”
—Anthony Ralphs, an events producer who dressed up as Darth Vader to ironically praise Flock at a San Diego City Council meeting, tells 404 Media why he sees parallels between the Dark Lord and the surveillance firm.
One More Thing
No one’s sure if synthetic mirror life will kill us all
  In February 2019, a group of scientists proposed a high-risk, cutting-edge, irresistibly exciting idea that the National Science Foundation should fund: making “mirror” bacteria.
These lab-created microbes would be organized like ordinary bacteria, but their proteins and sugars would be mirror images of those found in nature. Researchers believed they could reveal new insights into building cells, designing drugs, and even the origins of life.
But now, many of them have reversed course. They’ve become convinced that mirror organisms could trigger a catastrophic event threatening every form of life on Earth. Find out why they believe this could trigger a catastrophe.
—Stephen Ornes
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)

articles.title: Ex-Meta scientists want to bring visual AI to the factory floor | TechCrunch
articles.text:
AI is transforming everything around us but, thus far, it has largely remained contained to the digital realm. Increasingly, however, startups are looking to take it into the real world.
Perceptron, a startup started by two former Meta research scientists, is one such company. Founded in November 2024, the firm develops frontier vision models that aim to help machines more competently interact with their physical environments.
This week, the company launched its latest model, Isaac 0.5, which its creators say is designed to provide machines with the ability to “perceive, reason and act” in industrial settings. Specifically, the software is capable of helping vision-guided robots navigate complex environments like warehouses or factory floors. It also helps companies extract visual intelligence from videos recorded by those bots.
Isaac 0.5 is also being released as an open-weight model, so its parameters and training materials can be inspected by anyone.
The startup was co-founded by Armen Aghajanyan and Akshat Shrivastava, who previously worked for Meta’s Fundamental AI Research (FAIR), the tech giant’s AI research division. The duo see their software as the future of industrial automated deployment.
“Physical AI today forces a false choice: generalist foundation models that need multiple dedicated cloud GPUs for every instance, or narrow models that handle perception or control, but never both,” the company says.
Aghajanyan and Shrivastava say their tool is unlike existing models in the space because it is general-purpose, meaning that it’s not built for one specific, repetitive task. Instead, they say, the model is designed to be flexible depending on the particular environment (or situation) it is in.
In an interview, Shrivastava asked me to consider what goes into a simple physical process like organizing boxes: “Imagine there’s a robot being deployed to sort packages right now. What are the tasks it would need to do?”
Such a relatively simple task indeed consists of many steps. A robot would first have to read the label on the package, do some spatial analysis to understand where the boxes are, and decide which one to pick up. If it’s picking up a series of boxes, it would have to plan which boxes to pick up and in which order.
Perceptron’s software is designed to help robots find their way through each step of the process. To be clear, the industry already has software that can help machines do most of those tasks, but there are few programs that are designed to do it flexibly.
Where does the data for this algorithmic alchemy come from?
Models like Isaac 0.5 learn operational skills by ingesting gargantuan amounts of video training data. Perceptron says its new model was fed on a million hours of what is known as general video to teach its algorithm to identify particular settings, visuals, and scenarios. The company also relied heavily on what is known as ego video — video captured, typically through a GoPro or a wearable camera, from the perspective of a person completing a physical task — as well as UMI video, which are similarly used to teach AI systems movements by recording repetitive human actions.
While Perceptron isn’t disclosing the sources of its training data, Shrivastava said that the company had “internally built petabyte-scale datasets that span across modalities, whether it’s images, text, video, etc. all the way through robotic trajectories.”
The utility of a software that can help robots operate competently in warehouses is obviously vast, and Perceptron thinks it’s well-positioned to lead that wave of automation. The startup is ready to market its software to a variety of vendors, and thus potentially see its intelligence layer integrated into a broad array of industries.
Those industries include manufacturing, logistics and warehousing, security, mobility, as well as media and entertainment.
“Nothing like this really exists out there,” said Aghajanyan. “We’re really excited about it.”
The company previously raised $16 million from Bessemer Venture Partners, The Explorer Fund and SmartGateVC in 2024, according to Pitchbook. TechCrunch understands the startup is in the process of closing an additional round.
An earlier version of this story incorrectly reported recent funding details.

articles.title: Bundesbank will digitalen Euro und Wero kombinieren – doch ein Problem bleibt
articles.text:
Digitaler Euro soll in Wero-Wallet: Bundesbank plant Kombi gegen Paypal und Co.
Für mehr europäische Unabhängigkeit beim digitalen Bezahlen sollten aus Sicht der Bundesbank die europäische Paypal-Alternative Wero und der digitale Euro miteinander verzahnt werden. „Denkbar wäre beispielsweise, den digitalen Euro in die Wero Wallet zu integrieren“, sagte Bundesbank-Vorstand Lutz Lienenkämper in Frankfurt bei einem Symposium der Deutschen Bundesbank zum Zahlungsverkehr. „Das könnte die Reichweite europäischer Zahlungsangebote erhöhen und dazu beitragen, dass neue Lösungen nicht nebeneinanderstehen, sondern nahtlos zusammenwirken.“
Wero wird von der European Payments Initiative (EPI), einem Zusammenschluss von Banken und Zahlungsdienstleistern, vorangetrieben. Seit Anfang Juli 2024 bietet Wero nach dem Muster des US-Konkurrenten Paypal vor allem direkte mobile Geldzahlungen von Mensch zu Mensch an. Inzwischen kann Wero auch bei etlichen Händlern zum Einkaufen im Netz genutzt werden, ähnlich wie Kreditkarten, Apple Pay, Google Pay oder andere vergleichbare Dienste.
Wero-Nutzerzahlen sind noch gering
Nach jüngsten Angaben gibt es bislang 57 Millionen registrierte Wero-Nutzer in Belgien, Frankreich und Deutschland. An der Einführung in den Niederlanden, Luxemburg und Österreich wird gearbeitet. Noch habe Wero auch hierzulande das Potenzial nicht ausgeschöpft, stellte Lienenkämper fest. „Der Markthochlauf bleibt daher eine Aufgabe, die mit Nachdruck verfolgt werden muss.“
Der digitale Euro stößt auf Kritik
Dass die Europäische Zentralbank (EZB) parallel seit Jahren an einem digitalen Euro als Alternative zum Bargeld arbeitet, finden Kritiker auch angesichts der Kosten fragwürdig. Mit einem digitalen Euro wollen die Euro-Notenbanken privaten Anbietern vor allem aus den USA wie Paypal, Mastercard und Visa, die derzeit den Markt für digitale Zahlungen in Europa dominieren, ein europäisches Angebot entgegensetzen. Angepeilt ist die Einführung des digitalen Euro für 2029.
Der digitale Euro sei wichtig, sagte Lienenkämper: „Ein digitaler Euro ist Zentralbankgeld für den digitalen Raum: allgemein zugänglich, sicher, europäisch und mit hohem Datenschutz – als Ergänzung zu privaten Zahlungslösungen und auch zum Bargeld, nicht aber als deren Ersatz.“

articles.title: Nvidia is about to be a hundred-billion-dollar-a-quarter company
articles.text:
Nvidia’s predicting it will pull in $108 billion in revenue within just a few months. It wouldn’t be the first company to rake in over $100 billion in quarterly revenue — Amazon, Apple, and Alphabet have repeatedly reached the milestone.
Nvidia is about to be a hundred-billion-dollar-a-quarter company
The chip company made over $96 billion in the past quarter, most of it from its data center business.
Nvidia said in its latest earnings report that it brought in a record $96.2 billion in overall revenue in the past quarter, a jump of over $10 billion from the previous quarter. Its data center revenue alone more than doubled year-over-year to a record $89 billion, and the company’s profits more than doubled to $59.7 billion.
Nvidia’s “edge computing” category, which includes its consumer gaming business, accounted for just $7.2 billion of its revenue last quarter. That’s a 27 percent increase year-over-year, but Nvidia acknowledged that it experienced “slower consumer PC sales that were tempered by elevated memory and systems prices.” Component shortages continue to drive up prices for Nvidia’s consumer GPUs, and it also warned of price hikes for its AI chips ahead of Wednesday’s earnings report.

articles.title: BYD officialise la Great Seagull, une version agrandie de sa citadine électrique à moins de 20 000 €
articles.text:
Depuis plusieurs semaines, BYD distille des indices sur une nouvelle voiture 100 % électrique. Et justement, le constructeur chinois vient de lever un coin du voile sur ce projet à l’occasion du Salon de l’automobile de Chengdu, en donnant enfin son nom officiel : Great Seagull.
Comme l’a relayé le média CarNewsChina le 24 août 2026, ce futur modèle doit se glisser entre deux best-sellers de sa gamme Ocean : la citadine Seagull, vendue chez nous en Europe sous le nom de Dolphin Surf, et la compacte Dolphin « tout court ».
Une BYD Dolphin Surf en plus grand
Dans un premier teaser au mois de juillet, Zhang Zhuo, le directeur général du réseau commercial de la gamme Ocean chez BYD, avait publié sur les réseaux sociaux chinois une série de clichés volontairement flous, laissant deviner la silhouette d’un modèle encore jamais vu.
Pour accompagner ces photos, la description faisait une allusion explicite à une version plus grande de la Seagull/Dolphin Surf : « Alors que sa silhouette se dessine peu à peu dans l’ombre, la promesse de grandir est sur le point de se réaliser. » À ce moment-là, aucune information technique ni aucun nom n’avait filtré.
En parallèle de ces premières annonces, le dossier d’homologation déposé auprès du ministère chinois de l’Industrie et des Technologies de l’information (MIIT) a permis de lever une bonne partie du mystère.
On y apprend que la nouvelle venue affiche des dimensions nettement supérieures à celles de la Seagull actuelle : 4,21 m de longueur pour 1,81 m de large et 1,57 m de haut. L’empattement s’établit à 2,65 m.
Une BYD Dolphin qui accuse le poids des années
BYD n’a pour l’instant communiqué ni sur la capacité de la batterie, ni sur le prix de la future Great Seagull. Surtout, il reste à savoir si ce nouveau modèle intermédiaire sera également commercialisé en Europe. En tout cas, il tomberait à point nommé pour BYD, car l’actuelle Dolphin montre clairement des signes d’essoufflement. De plus, les dimensions entre les deux modèles sont quasi identiques.
Lancée en 2021 comme tout premier modèle de la famille Ocean, elle a certes bénéficié de quelques évolutions depuis, mais sa plateforme et sa présentation intérieure commencent à paraître datées face à des rivales plus récentes, à commencer par la MG4. Sur le plan esthétique, ses lignes arrondies et plutôt plates évoquent encore largement le style des débuts de la marque à l’export et ont pris un sacré coup de vieux.

articles.title: Ten years of UPI: The infrastructure that quietly rewrote how India lives
articles.text:
Ten years of UPI: The infrastructure that quietly rewrote how India lives
Ten years after its launch, UPI has become far more than a payment system. It has transformed everyday transactions, enabled commerce during the pandemic and taken India’s digital public infrastructure to the world.
In 2018, I moved back to Google to work on GPay. At the time, I could never have imagined that an instant real-time payment system developed in India by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) under the aegis of RBI with many notable individual contributions, would become so big and transform so much.
I remember trying to explain to colleagues abroad why a real-time, interoperable system built on a public utility model would work at a scale nothing else in the world had attempted. But ten years later, the undeniable proof is there for everyone to see.
UPI went far beyond a faster way to pay. It became the infrastructure underneath how more than a billion people's lives transformed, almost instantaneously.
The numbers alone tell part of that story: annual UPI transaction volume has gone from 1.78 crore in FY17 to over 24,162 crore in FY26, a nearly 13,000-fold increase, with transaction value rising from Rs 7,000 crore to around Rs 314 lakh crore in the same period, according to Ministry of Finance. In July 2026 alone, UPI recorded 2,366 crore transactions, the highest monthly volume in its decade-long journey.
Perhaps the clearest way to understand UPI’s social and economic impact is to remember the pandemic. India’s ability to navigate that period keeping households supported, small businesses functioning and everyday commerce moving, would have been materially harder without it.
As one of the world’s largest and most densely connected societies went into lockdown, the challenge was not only to contain a public health emergency but also to ensure that money could continue to move when people could not. At a time when people were sanitising groceries, parcels, door handles, and currency notes, handling cash had become another source of anxiety. This mattered especially for migrant workers who went back to their towns without any means to earn a living but many employers could support them through the ease of UPI payments. UPI made sure you didn't have to go anywhere. Groceries, medicines, a doctor's teleconsultation, rent, and even care packages, all of them got settled instantly.
What now feels ordinary was, at that moment, extraordinarily important. It made money fluid when people had to stay apart and helped preserve a measure of economic and social continuity in a year defined by uncertainty.
That same payment system has reshaped daily life well after the pandemic. Street vendors don't need cash and migrant workers send money home instantly. No more standing in queues and worrying about losing that hard earned daily wage. Now, the transformation has become invisible. We pay bills, split bills, pay school fees and even tip a delivery rider by just whipping out our phones and not thinking twice about what went behind it. It's not just the ease of use, but also the safety and dignity of those small daily decisions that used to carry real cost in more ways than one.
UPI now processes over 20 billion transactions a month, across 504 million users and 65 million merchants, accounting for 84% of India's digital retail payments and nearly half of all real-time payment volume globally, according to BCG/NPCI Global Benchmark Report.
No other country has built anything close to this at this speed. That scale has also meant deeper institutional reach: the number of banks live on UPI has grown from 44 in FY17 to 703 today, according to Ministry of Finance.
Not just spending, but that same shift has also happened when it comes to how India invests. The retail SIP transactions in India through UPI grew by almost 177% last year alone. Free and fast flow of money through UPI has been helpful for the growth of both mutual funds and broking transactions as everyone has easy access from their mobile phones. That's financial inclusion actually happening, not as policy language, but as habit.
And this gargantuan success is now transforming other countries. For the past many decades now, India was perceived as the biggest exporter of finished digital products, engineers and IT services. UPI has taken that story and levelled it up. India is now exporting the underlying infrastructure itself. UPI is already live in eight-plus countries, including the UAE, Singapore, France and the UK, according to Ministry of Finance.
We have signed digital public infrastructure cooperation agreements with 23 nations, with cross-border UPI volumes growing 20x in a single year, according to NPCI International/PIB data on UPI's global footprint and cross-border transaction growth, FY23–FY25.
When the CEO of PayPal, one of the pioneers of online transactions, said "everywhere I go, India comes up," he wasn't far from the truth. UPI is the first, and possibly the biggest, payment system integrated into the PayPal World. Countries aren't just admiring what India built, but going a step further and partnering with us to build it for them.
It's about more than just payments. This is a real, working demonstration that India can conceive, build, and scale deep technology infrastructure, not just service it for others, at a level the rest of the world now studies and adopts. It's a much-needed reminder that capability does not need to stay contained to a single sector. We are capable of applying the engineering discipline, design thinking, and scale-first approach that built UPI to achieving India’s ambitions for the future. These can be in AI or anything else.
The next decade will see UPI go beyond being just a payment rail. The most immediate shift is likely to be international. Imagine a global UPI that makes remittances and merchant payments across countries as instant and inexpensive as domestic ones.
However, the strongest foundation for the next phase can be built on the domestic front. Credit on UPI is the frontier waiting to be unlocked. Contextual lending could genuinely change spending power for first-time borrowers. When commerce becomes more fluid, the economy becomes more productive.
Beyond that, there are three quieter shifts that are worth watching. The first, I expect, will be conversational, AI-led payments that let people transact in the language they already think in.
The next one that comes to mind is the extension of this power of payments to the offline world, to places the internet is yet to penetrate. And then comes the biggest change - programmable money that lets payments execute themselves when their conditions are met.
Smart-contract-like rules could automate conditional payments, while machine-to-machine and IoT micro-payments are already allowing devices, vehicles and software agents to pay one another securely in real time. This is bound to get more sophisticated. Maybe your fridge will order and pay for your groceries. If built with the same principles of interoperability, trust and inclusion, these innovations will not merely add features to UPI, but will expand what financial infrastructure can do for India, and increasingly, the world.
Ten years in, UPI’s real achievement won’t be the volumes, staggering as they are. It will be that an entire generation of Indians now expect their financial lives to simply work—instantly, safely, and without friction. I suspect the next decade will be about proving that India can build that same expectation into everything else it touches.
(Ambarish Kenghe is the Group Chief Executive Officer at Angel One )

articles.title: Smart Glasses: Was gegen Erkennung schützen soll
articles.text:
Smart Glasses und Überwachungskameras: Wie Aktivisten mit Kleidung dagegen angehen
Versuche, einer potenziellen Überwachung durch Kameras mit spezieller Kleidung zu entgehen, sind nicht neu. Doch die durch KI optimierte Gesichtserkennung sowie der aktuelle Streit um die Smart Glasses von Meta machen entsprechende Ansätze wieder populär.
KI-Algorithmen verwirren
Konkret geht es dabei darum, KI-Algorithmen in die Irre zu führen, wie Futurezone berichtet. Dazu dienen etwa wiederkehrende Muster im Gesicht wie die Augen-Nase-Partie, nach denen die Systeme suchen. Finden sich solche Muster in großer Zahl auf der Kleidung, sollen die Kamerasysteme nicht mehr genau entscheiden können, was das eigentliche menschliche Gesicht ist.
Entsprechende Produkte bietet etwa das Leipziger Label Urban Privacy an. Das Team habe sich das Tarnprinzip von Kriegsschiffen aus dem Ersten Weltkrieg abgeschaut, wie die Designerin Nicole Scheller erklärt. Dabei sollte der gegnerischen Partei die Abschätzung von Entfernung und Geschwindigkeit mit starken grafischen Mustern und kontrastierenden Farben erschwert werden.
Frisuren und Kleidung gegen Gesichtserkennung
Dieses sogenannte Dazzle-Camouflage-Prinzip zum Täuschen von Überwachungskameras setzen Aktivist:innen wie der US-amerikanische Künstler Adam Harvey auch bei Frisuren und Schminke ein. Dadurch sollen die Haare stärkere Muster aufweisen als die Gesichter der Personen – und somit die Algorithmen durcheinanderbringen.
Allerdings weisen Expert:innen wie Urban-Privacy-Designer Daniel Preuß darauf hin, dass Kleidung und Frisuren ihre Träger:innen nicht unsichtbar machen können. Die Kleidung könne „Störsignale senden, helfen, mehr Informationen in das System zu geben, als tatsächlich da sind, und möglicherweise die Erkennung verlangsamen“, wie Preuß laut Futurezone betont.
Die IT-Sicherheitsforscherin Katharina Krombholz vom CISPA Helmholtz-Zentrum für Informationssicherheit warnt sogar davor, dass ein „Gefühl der falschen Sicherheit“ entstehen könnte. Letztlich wisse man nicht genau, wie die Systeme funktionieren. Eine Garantie dafür, dass ein Gesicht wegen der Ablenkungsmanöver aussortiert wird, gibt es daher nicht.
Smart Glasses droht Verbot
Metas Smart Glasses droht derweil in Deutschland ein Verbot. Denn die Möglichkeit, heimlich in der Öffentlichkeit zu filmen, bedeutet laut Expert:innen einen Verstoß gegen das hiesige Datenschutzrecht.

articles.title: "Le dernier argument face à Google Maps s'effondre" : Apple impose ses publicités dans Plans, et la colère monte
articles.text:
"Le dernier argument face à Google Maps s'effondre" : Apple impose ses publicités dans Plans, et la colère monte
Ça y est, c'est fait. Apple a glissé des publicités dans Plans, son application de cartographie. Le déploiement a démarré aux États-Unis et au Canada, aucune option de désactivation n'existe, et les abonnés payants encaissent mal la nouvelle.
Le projet, que nous évoquions déjà en février 2025, a pris forme. Apple a confirmé au site 9to5Mac que les premières publicités apparaissent dans Plans depuis le 25 août, avec une montée en charge progressive dans les semaines à venir. Plus d'un milliard de recherches commerciales transitent chaque mois par l'application, selon Apple. Une requête sur deux débouche sur une action concrète.
Enchères au mot-clé, badge bleu et zéro opt-out
Les annonces se glissent à deux endroits : dans les "Lieux suggérés" dès l'ouverture du champ de recherche, et en tête des résultats après une requête. Un badge bleu "Ad" les signale, à raison d'une seule publicité par recherche. Le système repose sur des enchères par mot-clé, sans budget minimum.
Pour attirer les premiers commerces, Apple accorde 15 % de crédit mensuel (plafonné à 1 000 dollars) pendant un an aux inscrits avant le 11 octobre 2026. Certaines catégories restent bannies : services à domicile, jeux d'argent, alcool, cryptomonnaies, religion.
Sur Reddit, la pilule passe mal. Un abonné Apple One à 50 dollars par mois résume l'amertume générale : "Ce que j'adore, c'est de payer 50 dollars par mois et de voir quand même des pubs dans Plans et News."
	
Ce que j'adore, c'est de payer 50 dollars par mois d'Apple One et de voir quand même des pubs dans Plans et News.
Plusieurs internautes soulignent que l'absence de publicité était le dernier argument tangible de Plans face à Google Maps et Waze, deux applications déjà truffées d'annonces mais autrement plus complètes. "Google Maps est largement plus précis et fonctionnel. Le seul avantage de Plans, c'était l'absence de pub", tranche un autre.
La perspective d'un futur palier "sans pub" facturé plus cher, sur le modèle de YouTube Premium ou des offres TV, revient dans les commentaires comme une quasi-certitude. Un constat plus structurel circule aussi : Apple anticiperait une érosion de ses commissions sur les achats intégrés, fragilisées par les régulations européennes et américaines, et chercherait à compenser via la publicité.
La France épargnée, pour l'instant
Le déploiement reste cantonné à l'Amérique du Nord, sans calendrier pour l'Europe. En février 2026, la Commission européenne a estimé que Plans et Apple Ads ne constituaient pas des passerelles suffisamment importantes au sens du Digital Markets Act, faute d'audience sur le continent. Apple dispose donc d'une latitude réglementaire confortable pour étendre le dispositif, d'autant que la plateforme Ads on Maps s'appuie sur Apple Business, actif dans plus de 200 pays depuis avril 2026. L'infrastructure est prête, seul le calendrier manque.

articles.title: Registrar tu móvil en un control de tráfico: qué pueden hacer la Policía o Guardia Civil y cuándo pueden acceder a tus datos
articles.text:
Vamos a explicarte en qué casos un agente puede acceder a los datos de tu móvil cuando están haciendo un registro. Tanto la Policía como la Guardia Civil van a poder retener tu dispositivo en algunos casos, pero otra cosa diferente es acceder a sus datos.
Por eso, vamos a decirte las diferencias entre cuándo pueden retener tu dispositivo y cuándo acceder a los datos. También te diremos cómo te protege la Constitución Española, y las excepciones en las que sí podrían acceder a los archivos de tu smartphone.
Retener tu dispositivo sí, acceder a tus datos no
Los dos aspectos clave que conviene diferenciar son el retener tu dispositivo y el acceder a los datos de este. La Ley de Seguridad Ciudadana (LO 4/2015), en sus artículos 16 a 19, permite que los agentes puedan identificar personas y realizar comprobaciones o registros en sus bienes y vehículos para prevenir delitos.
Esto quiere decir que la Policía o la Guardia Civil podrían incautar tu móvil si tienen algún indicio de que esté vinculado con un delito grave, pudiéndolo asegurar como una prueba natural. Vamos, que lo pueden coger e incluso se lo pueden llevar.
Pero otra cosa diferente es acceder a él. Encender la pantalla de tu móvil y explorar sus archivos no es tan fácil, y van a necesitar una autorización judicial previa y motivada, tal y como establece el artículo 288 sexies c de la Ley de Enjuiciamiento Criminal. Esto lo respalda la sentencia 489/2018 del Tribunal Supremo, que diferencia entre incautar el hardware y leer chats o volcar datos.
¿Y por qué? Pues por la Constitución Española, que en su artículo 18.1 garantiza tu derecho a la intimidad, y en el 18.3 protege el secreto de tus comunicaciones. Además, el artículo 18.4 limita el uso de la informática para garantizar el honor.
Qué pasa si enseñas la app de miDGT
Desde hace unos años tenemos la app de miDGT, que es oficial y permite usarse cuando quieras enseñarle a un policía tu permiso de conducir. Porque esto sí te lo pueden pedir, y si no lo tienes en formato físico puedes usar esta aplicación. Esto supone darles el móvil para que la miren y la comprueben.
En este caso, enseñar tu documentación en la pantalla de tu móvil no le da a los agentes permiso para revisar el resto del dispositivo. Vamos, que no van a poder cerrar esa aplicación y ponerse a abrir otras.
No te pueden obligar a entregar el móvil desbloqueado
Por último, en el caso de que seamos conductores y nos hayan parado para inspeccionarnos, no tenemos la obligación de entregar el móvil desbloqueado durante esta parada.
De la misma manera, tampoco te pueden multar por negarte a darles acceso a tu teléfono móvil. Vamos, que no pueden obligarte a que les enseñes nada de tu dispositivo, ni el contenido de tus archivos ni el de otra aplicación.
Existen algunas excepciones
Eso sí, también existen algunas excepciones muy limitadas, casos concretos en los que sí podrían acceder al contenido de tu dispositivo. Son los siguientes:
- Consentimiento inequívoco: Si accedes de forma voluntaria y consciente a desbloquear tu smartphone a petición del agente, el registro será válido. Vamos, que te lo pueden pedir, pero tú podrás negarte o acceder a hacerlo.
- Urgencia ante delitos flagrantes: El artículo 588 sexies c.4 de la Ley de Enjuiciamiento Criminal permite a la Policía Judicial examinar los datos de tu móvil en casos de urgencia ante delitos flagrantes. Eso sí, si lo hacen, los agentes tendrán la obligación de comunicárselo a un juez en menos de 24 horas.
Con el segundo dato, debe quedar clara una cosa. No pueden pedirte acceder a tu móvil en un control de velocidad o alcohol, esto nunca justifica esta medida. Tendrá que tratarse de otro caso, y cuando estés cometiendo un delito flagrante.

articles.title: Peter Otobong: From Coder to Fintech Systems Engineer | TechCabal
articles.text:
The technology was not the problem.
For Peter Otobong and his team at Fraqtion Finance, the idea was simple enough: allow people to pool money to finance real-world trade, such as a Chinese company buying lithium from Nigeria. The software could be built. The architecture could be designed. The engineers could make the system work.
But then came the questions that code could not answer.
Who would license it? Who would regulate it? Where would the capital come from? Which financial institutions would support it? And how would the technology fit into the systems that already governed the movement of money and commodities across borders?
The project never launched.
For Otobong, however, its failure became one of the most important lessons of his career.
“The biggest constraints are not necessarily technical. The biggest constraints are normally the systems in which the technology is going to operate in,” he says.
It was a lesson that would change the way he looked at his profession. Technology, he began to understand, does not exist in isolation. A piece of software may work perfectly and still fail if the business around it is wrong, if regulation does not permit it, if institutions cannot support it or if the people it was built for cannot use it.
For someone who had once dreamed of becoming a mad scientist, it was an important realisation.
As a boy, Otobong had imagined science as an almost limitless frontier. He wanted to build things, explore strange possibilities and push beyond what was already known.
“A scientist who is doing a lot of stuff, like going to space, trying to imitate aliens,” he says, recalling the kind of scientist he wanted to become.
The inspiration came largely from the cartoons and animations he watched growing up. They gave him a world in which imagination was not constrained by what was immediately possible.
Years later, that instinct to build remains. But the problems Otobong is interested in have become more complicated.
He is no longer simply asking whether something can be built.
He wants to know whether it can survive the world around it.
And that distinction has taken him from tinkering with computers as a child to writing software, building blockchain systems, developing communities of African technologists and working on financial infrastructure for businesses moving money across borders.
Finding a path into tech
The computer laboratory at his primary school was supposed to teach Otobong how to use a computer. Instead, it left him wondering how the machine itself worked.
In Primary Four, his school began taking students to the laboratory to learn basic applications such as Microsoft Word and Excel. While other pupils were learning how to use the programmes, Otobong found himself more interested in what was happening beneath the screen.
“That was where my interests in computers really grew,” he says. “It was my first physical interaction with this imagination I’ve always had to become sort of a mad scientist.”
The laptop that would finally give that curiosity somewhere to go came years later.
In 2014, an uncle gave him one, and for the first time, Otobong had a computer he could explore on his own. He began teaching himself how to code, moving from curiosity about computers to actually building things with them.
“2014 was when I actually started getting my hands dirty with C++ and writing code and also getting introduced to how to design web applications,” he says.
Yet even then, software engineering did not feel like a career to him.
He had grown up in an environment where the profession was barely visible. The people around him followed careers he could easily name: government work, accounting, engineering and jobs in the oil industry. Software was something he enjoyed experimenting with, but he had never seen anyone close to him turn that interest into a profession.
“I grew up in an environment where it was very strange to say somebody’s a software engineer,” he says. “I don’t have any relative or friend who was into IT.”
So, when the time came to choose a university course in 2015, Otobong did what many young Nigerians do when the path ahead is still unclear: he followed a familiar route that still left room for his curiosity.
A family friend introduced him to electrical and electronics engineering at the University of Port Harcourt, Rivers State in Southern Nigeria. The course offered a bridge between the physical systems that fascinated him and the computers he had begun teaching himself to understand.
For the next five years, he studied the discipline. But it was outside the classroom, during an internship, that Otobong would begin to understand where he truly belonged.
From hardware to software
In 2019, Otobong interned at Atopets Automation, a robotics and automation company in Port Harcourt. He worked with microcontrollers, Arduino boards, ESPs and Raspberry Pi, building systems that could respond to the physical world.
But he found himself increasingly drawn to the software behind the hardware.
“I discovered that I love the hardware, but I also love the process of writing software to make the hardware work,” he says.
That realisation pushed him deeper into software and shaped his final-year project: a facial-recognition system that could identify authorised users and control access to a smart door.
Then, in 2020, he was selected as a Google Student Developer Lead at the University of Port Harcourt. The programme exposed him to developers across Africa and, for the first time, showed him that software engineering could be a viable career.
“I got to see people who were in the software field as a full-time career, and they were doing well,” he says. “And so it just changed something in my mind because I can now see that I can actually build a career out of this.”
From building systems to building communities
After graduating in 2021, Otobong’s first professional break came at the African Blockchain Centre for Developers (ABCD). A friend had told him about a blockchain training programme, and he applied, initially expecting to learn alongside other young developers.
He was selected as one of the first 14 people in the cohort. But ABCD soon realised that Otobong was bringing more to the programme than a willingness to learn. He already had experience with technology and, importantly, with bringing people together around it.
“They reached out and asked if I wanted to join the team, not just to learn about blockchain, but to work on the technical side and with other developers.”
The invitation marked a subtle shift in his career. Otobong entered ABCD as a learner but soon found himself on the other side of the learning process, working as a technical and developer advocate.
At first, his work centred on understanding blockchain technologies such as Ethereum and helping others make sense of a field that was still unfamiliar to many developers in Nigeria. But as ABCD’s work evolved from training and advocacy to building software and tools for clients in the blockchain space, so did Otobong’s responsibilities.
He began working with organisations to define what they needed, translate those needs into technical requirements and scope projects. He also helped vet developers, write code and coordinate technical teams.
The progression was gradual, but significant. He was no longer simply learning how technology worked; he was learning how to make it work for other people.
Eventually, Otobong grew into a technical lead role, taking greater responsibility for technical delivery while helping organisations find, evaluate and manage the developers who would build their products.
It was around this time that another idea began taking shape in his mind: technology was not only about the things you built. It was also about the people and communities that made building possible.
Building a community
While at ABCD, Otobong became interested in Blacks In Technology, a global non-profit that supports Black people pursuing careers in technology. A friend regularly posted about the organisation, prompting him to reach out to Dennis Schultz, an executive director.
Otobong told Schultz about his experience leading the Google community at the University of Port Harcourt, his work at ABCD and an impact project he wanted to pursue.
The conversation led to a call with Schultz, which opened the door for him to establish a Blacks In Technology chapter in Nigeria.
One of his first priorities was helping developers who wanted to get started but lacked the equipment to do so. The idea was personal. His own journey in tech had started with the HP Mini laptop his uncle gave him in 2014, so he wanted to give other developers a similar opportunity.
“They approved $10,000 to support us in buying some used laptops,” he says. “But each time they tried to send the money to Nigeria, it was flagged for risk and then reversed. It happened on three occasions.”
The failed transfers meant the laptop project could not go ahead, so Otobong and the chapter turned to events, programmes and online learning opportunities instead.
“We had to focus on doing events and programmes, sometimes virtually. We would get vouchers because back then BIT had a lot of partnerships with the likes of Coursera and other different platforms.”
Otobong says the approach helped the community grow. Within a short period, he says the Nigerian chapter had close to 500 members and was recognised as the fastest-growing international chapter in 2022.
The experience also changed how Otobong thought about creating impact in technology. He began to see that building the people around technology was as important as building the technology itself.
“The most important way to build impact or create value is to build community and ecosystems.”
For Otobong, communities create the talent and opportunities that allow an ecosystem to grow.
“We can’t build in silos. Community is the best tool for shaping the ecosystem. And when you shape the ecosystem, what you do is that you also shape and build the talent.”
Building for a different reality
In 2023, Otobong left ABCD and spent several months thinking about what he wanted to do next. He was unsure whether to continue pursuing software engineering or move towards something more focused on business and strategy.
“I was thinking, should I still try to look for new opportunities and jobs to just go deep into tech, or should I pivot into something that has more business- and strategy-related, or just try to become a founder of something else?” he said.
He eventually chose to stay in technology. In January 2024, he joined LTO Network, a Dutch blockchain company focused on real-world assets, as a senior software engineer.
At LTO, he worked on systems that allowed assets such as land and legal documents to be represented on the blockchain. One of the projects was GoLand Registry, which was designed to allow property owners to create verifiable records of their assets and use them to access financing.
Otobong’s role was to help adapt the platform for Burkina Faso. That meant thinking beyond the technology itself: how people would use it, how it would work with limited internet access and how it could fit into existing government processes.
“I had a lot of autonomy at LTO where I could think through problems, I could create an architecture, I could present it to the team, and they would decide what the best approach was.”
The work exposed him to a different kind of engineering problem. The challenge was no longer simply whether something could be built, but whether it could work in the environment for which it was intended.
GoLand had been developed in collaboration with the United Nations for Afghanistan before being adapted for Burkina Faso. Otobong says its adoption depended not only on the technology, but also on government support and existing administrative systems.
LTO was also where Otobong built the project he is most proud of in his career: a relay protocol that allowed wallets to communicate with one another and exchange files and other assets, rather than just cryptocurrency.
“I would say it was something I was proud of because people were using it. So, when I see people look at their wallet balances and some people have a lot of their money inside the wallet, and they are really looking forward to the progress, when is this going to go live? Just knowing that you are building something that has value and you know has like a long-term use case for a lot of people made me really proud.”
After his time at LTO, Otobong joined Esca Finance, a fintech focused on cross-border payments, foreign exchange and liquidity for businesses in emerging markets, in 2026 in a full-time role. He now works on cross-border finance and liquidity, as the company builds financial rails to help businesses manage currency conversions and reduce their exposure to foreign exchange volatility.
His work there draws on the experiences that have shaped his career so far. Beyond building the technology, he has had to understand the financial system in which it operates, including compliance, fraud mitigation and the processes involved in verifying customers and businesses.
“I have learned that being a software engineer is not just about being technical, I have to also understand the domain in which I am operating.”
From software engineer to systems thinker
Looking back across his career, Otobong can identify things he would have done differently. Chief among them is that he wishes he had challenged himself earlier — and dreamed bigger.
“I really wished that I had challenged myself more. Let’s say it’s one of my regrets.”
For a while, he says, he kept too many options open instead of committing fully to a particular direction. He watched some of his friends go deep into fields such as artificial intelligence while he remained interested in the connections between different technologies.
It is not that he believes he chose the wrong path. If anything, he has become more convinced that his path was right. What he regrets is not pursuing it with enough conviction.
“It’s not because the path I chose was wrong; my path is still very correct, but I feel like I should have had more conviction.”
That conviction has also changed what he believes it means to be a software engineer.
When he began writing code as a teenager, the computer was the thing he wanted to understand. Over the years, the questions have become larger. He now thinks about the businesses, institutions, regulations and people that software must work with before it can create any meaningful impact.
It is a shift from seeing technology as a tool to seeing it as part of a larger system — one that can succeed only when the pieces around it work, too.
At ESCA Finance, that is the perspective he brings to his work in cross-border finance and liquidity. It is also the clearest expression yet of the engineer he has become: not someone concerned only with whether the code works, but with whether the system it powers can work.
“As much as I call myself a software engineer, I would say I see myself as a systems engineer. Because I am no longer just thinking about software as code, but I’m thinking about software as systems.”
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks.
